\[\psi_S=\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}dq_i\wedge dp_i(\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\eta)=\boldsymbol\xi^T\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}J^{(i)}\right)\boldsymbol\eta=\boldsymbol\xi^TJ\boldsymbol\eta.\]

corrected_json.proof_discussion_latex:
Computing the 2-form,
\[dQ_i\wedge dP_i=dq_i\wedge dP_i+hm_i^{-1}dP_i\wedge dP_i;\]
but $du\wedge du\equiv0$ for any $u$, hence
\[dQ_i\wedge dP_i=dq_i\wedge dP_i;\]
and (2.21) implies
\[dQ_i\wedge dP_i=dq_i\wedge dp_i-h\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_i\wedge\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial q_j\partial q_i}dq_j.\]
It is then a simple exercise to show that
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_i\wedge\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial q_j\partial q_i}dq_j=0,\]
using the skew-symmetry of the wedge product and the fact that the Hessian matrix is symmetric.

corrected_json.statement_latex:
Let
\[H_1(\boldsymbol q,\boldsymbol p)=\boldsymbol p^TM^{-1}\boldsymbol p/2,\qquad H_2(\boldsymbol q,\boldsymbol p)=U(\boldsymbol q),\]
then a splitting method for $H=H_1+H_2$ may be obtained by determining the flow maps for each of the two parts. For $H_1$ we have the differential equations
\[\dot{\boldsymbol q}=M^{-1}\boldsymbol p,\qquad\dot{\boldsymbol p}=\boldsymbol0.\]
The second equation tells us that $\boldsymbol p$ is constant, so it is fixed at its initial value, whereas the first equation says that $\boldsymbol q$ evolves on a linear path, hence its flow map is
\[\boldsymbol Q=\boldsymbol q+hM^{-1}\boldsymbol p,\qquad\boldsymbol P=\boldsymbol p.\]

corrected_json.label: Example 2.5 (Verlet is Symplectic)
corrected_json.statement_latex:
For the Symplectic Euler method $\mathcal G_h$ and its adjoint method $\mathcal G_h^\dagger$, consider the composition
\[\mathcal K_h:=\mathcal G_{h/2}^\dagger\circ\mathcal G_{h/2}.\]
corrected_json.proof_latex:
Let
\[\begin{bmatrix}\bar{\boldsymbol q}\\\bar{\boldsymbol p}\end{bmatrix}=\mathcal G_{h/2}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol q\\\boldsymbol p\end{bmatrix},\]
i.e.,
\[\bar{\boldsymbol q}=\boldsymbol q+(h/2)M^{-1}\bar{\boldsymbol p},\qquad\bar{\boldsymbol p}=\boldsymbol p-(h/2)\nabla U(\boldsymbol q).\]
and set
\[\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol Q\\\boldsymbol P\end{bmatrix}=\mathcal G_{h/2}^\dagger\begin{bmatrix}\bar{\boldsymbol q}\\\bar{\boldsymbol p}\end{bmatrix},\]
i.e.,
\[\boldsymbol Q=\bar{\boldsymbol q}+(h/2)M^{-1}\bar{\boldsymbol p},\qquad\boldsymbol P=\bar{\boldsymbol p}-(h/2)\nabla U(\boldsymbol Q).\]
The composition simplifies to
\[\bar{\boldsymbol p}=\boldsymbol p-\frac h2\nabla U(\boldsymbol q),\qquad\boldsymbol Q=\boldsymbol q+hM^{-1}\bar{\boldsymbol p},\qquad\boldsymbol P=\bar{\boldsymbol p}-\frac h2\nabla U(\boldsymbol Q).\]
This is just the leapfrog/Verlet method in its Hamiltonian form.

corrected_json.statement_latex:
To see that it is symplectic, we first note that this is a symmetric composition of the form
\[\mathcal K_h=\mathcal G_{h/2}^{\dagger}\circ\mathcal G_{h/2},\]
where $\mathcal G_h$ is defined by
\[P=p-h\nabla_qH(q,P),\tag{2.29}\]
\[Q=q+h\nabla_pH(q,P),\tag{2.30}\]
so it is enough to show that this basic method is symplectic.
corrected_json.proof_latex:
Taking differentials of (2.30) defining $\mathcal G_h$ and then wedge products and summing, we have
\[\sum_i dQ_i\wedge dP_i=\sum_i dq_i\wedge dP_i+h\sum_i\sum_j H_{p_iq_j}dq_j\wedge dP_i+h\sum_i\sum_j H_{p_ip_j}dP_j\wedge dP_i.\]
The last term on the right vanishes by equality of mixed partials and the antisymmetry of the wedge product. On the other hand, using (2.29), we obtain, by similar means,
\[\sum_i dq_i\wedge dP_i=\sum_i dq_i\wedge dp_i-h\sum_i\sum_j H_{q_ip_j}dq_i\wedge dP_j.\]
Relabelling the indices in this sum and using our previous work results in
\[\sum_i dQ_i\wedge dP_i=\sum_i dq_i\wedge dp_i,\]
implying that the method is symplectic.

corrected_json.statement_latex: We can express the fundamental consequence as follows: not only are Hamiltonian flow maps symplectic, but also near-identity symplectic maps are (in an approximate sense) Hamiltonian flow maps [31]. The fact leads to the existence of a modified (perturbed) Hamiltonian from which the discrete trajectory may be derived (as snapshots of continuous trajectories). In some cases we may derive this perturbed Hamiltonian as an expansion in powers of the stepsize.

corrected_json.label: Theorem 3.1
corrected_json.statement_latex:
Theorem 3.1. Suppose the Hamiltonian $H$ and modified Hamiltonian $\bar H_k$ are smooth functions globally defined on a convex, compact subset $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^{2N_c}$ and suppose that the exact solution and numerical approximations (for $h$ sufficiently small) are confined to $\mathcal B$. Then, we have asymptotically for $h\to0$ that
\[H(\boldsymbol z_n)=H(\boldsymbol z_0)+O(h^r),\]
for $n=0,1,\ldots,\nu$ where $\tau=\nu h=O(h^{-k+r})$.
corrected_json.proof_latex:
Proof First observe that due to smoothness and the assumptions on $\mathcal B$, we have a global Lipschitz constant
\[|H(\boldsymbol u)-H(\boldsymbol v)|< L\|\boldsymbol u-\boldsymbol v\|\]
for all $\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v\in\mathcal B$.
Denote by $\mathcal F_h^{(k)}$ the flow map of the truncated Hamiltonian expansion $\bar H_k$,
\[\mathcal F_h^{(k)}\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}=\exp(h\mathcal L_{\bar H_k}).\]
By construction, we have
\[\boldsymbol z_{n+1}=\mathcal F_h^{(k)}(\boldsymbol z_n)+\boldsymbol\eta_n\]
where $\|\boldsymbol\eta_n\|\le Ch^{k+1}$.
Since $\mathcal F_h^{(k)}$ preserves its Hamiltonian (3.11), we have
\[\bar H_k(\mathcal F_h^{(k)}(\boldsymbol z_n))=\widetilde H_k(\boldsymbol z_n).\]
Now
\[\begin{aligned}\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_\nu)-\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_0)
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\nu-1}\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_{n+1})-\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_n)\\
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\nu-1}\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_{n+1})-\widetilde H_k(\mathcal F_h^{(k)}(\boldsymbol z_n))\\
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\nu-1}\bar H_k(\mathcal F_h^{(k)}(\boldsymbol z_n)+\boldsymbol\eta_n)-\bar H_k(\mathcal F_h^{(k)}(\boldsymbol z_n)).\end{aligned}\]
Hence
\[|\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_\nu)-\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_0)|\le L\sum_{n=0}^{\nu-1}\|\boldsymbol\eta_n\|\le L\nu h^{k+1}.\]
We have $\nu=\tau/h$, thus
\[|\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_\nu)-\bar H_k(\boldsymbol z_0)|\le L\tau h^k.\]
Next observe that
\[H=\bar H_k-h^rH_{(r)}-h^{r+1}H_{(r+1)}-\cdots-h^kH_{(k)}=\bar H_k+O(h^r).\]
Therefore
\[|H(\boldsymbol z_\nu)-H(\boldsymbol z_0)|\le L\nu h^{k+1}+O(h^r),\]
so that, as long as $\nu\le C_2h^{-k+r-1}$, we have
\[|H(\boldsymbol z_\nu)-H(\boldsymbol z_0)|\le O(h^r).\quad\square\]

corrected_json.statement_latex:
Definition 3.1 (Affine Invariance) Let
\[\frac{\mathrm d\boldsymbol z}{\mathrm dt}=f(\boldsymbol z)\tag{3.16}\]
be a given ordinary differential equation. The transformation $\widetilde{\boldsymbol z}=A\boldsymbol z$, where $A$ is a non-singular square matrix, results in the modified differential equation
\[\frac{\mathrm d\boldsymbol z}{\mathrm dt}=Af(A^{-1}\widetilde{\boldsymbol z}).\tag{3.17}\]
Let $z_0,z_1,\ldots$ be a sequence of points obtained by application of the numerical method $\mathcal G_h$ to (3.16). If the same method, when applied to (3.17) produces the set of points $Az_0,Az_1,\ldots$, then we say that the numerical method is invariant with respect to the transformation $\widetilde{\boldsymbol z}=Az$. An affine invariant method is one which is invariant under any such transformation.

This follows from the antisymmetry of the wedge product $(\mathrm dx\wedge\mathrm dy=-\mathrm dy\wedge\mathrm dx)$, and the fact that the Hessian matrix of $U$ is symmetric. Next, note that
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\sum_{k=1}^{l}\mathrm dq_i\wedge\lambda_k\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}(g_k^{\prime\prime})_{ij}\mathrm dq_j=\sum_{k=1}^{l}\lambda_k\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\mathrm dq_i\wedge\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}(g_k^{\prime\prime})_{ij}\mathrm dq_j=0,\]
by the same reasoning, since each of $g_k^{\prime\prime}$ is a symmetric matrix. Finally
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\sum_{k=1}^{l}[\mathrm dq_i\wedge(\mathrm d\lambda_k)g_{ki}^{\prime}=\sum_{k=1}^{l}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}g_{ki}^{\prime}\mathrm dq_i\right)\wedge\mathrm d\lambda_k=\sum_{k=1}^{l}\mathrm dg_k\wedge\mathrm d\lambda_k=0,\]
since we know that $\mathrm dg_k=0$ from (4.13). Therefore
\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\mathrm dq_i\wedge\mathrm dp_i=0.\]

corrected_json.label: Lemma 4.1
corrected_json.statement_latex:
Lemma 4.1 Let $\gamma:\mathbb R^{N_c}\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Let $q,p\in\mathbb R^{N_c}$ be constrained to the manifold defined by
\[\gamma(q)=0,\quad p\cdot\nabla\gamma(q)=0,\]
and suppose $P,\mu$ satisfy $P=p-\mu\nabla\gamma(q)$. Then
\[\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge dP_j=\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge dp_j.\]
corrected_json.proof_latex:
Clearly the result follows provided
\[\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge d[\mu\nabla\gamma(q)]_j=0,\]
where $[\ldots]_j$ indicates the jth component of the term in brackets. We have
\[\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge d[\mu\nabla\gamma(q)]_j=\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge\left(\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial q_j}d\mu+\mu\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\gamma''_{ij}dq_j\right).\]
Then we note
\[\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial q_j}d\mu=\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial q_j}dq_j\wedge d\mu=0,\]
since $\gamma(q)\equiv0$ implies $d\gamma(q)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial q_j}dq_j\equiv0$. Moreover
\[\sum_{j=1}^{N_c}dq_j\wedge\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\gamma''_{ij}dq_j=0,\]
since the Hessian matrix $\gamma''$ is symmetric.

DLM Rigid Body Molecular Dynamics Step
1. “Kick”: update the momenta and angular momentum vectors with known forces and torques for a half step:
\[p^k:=p^k+\tfrac h2 F^k,\quad\pi^k:=\pi^k+\tfrac h2\tau^k.\]
2. “Drift”: step forward a whole step in positions
\[q^k:=q^k+hp^k.\]
3. “Spin”: update the rotational state of the kth rigid body by the sequence of steps
\[\Theta:=\Theta^x(\tfrac h2\pi_1^k/I_1);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T,\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^y(\tfrac h2\pi_2^k/I_2);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T,\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^z(h\pi_3^k/I_3);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T,\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^y(\tfrac h2\pi_2^k/I_2);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T,\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^x(\tfrac h2\pi_1^k/I_1);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T.\]
4. “Kick”: update the momenta and angular momentum vectors (as in Step 1) with a half step using new forces $F^k$ and torques $\tau^k$ evaluated at the current $q,\Theta$.

corrected_json.statement_latex:
DLM Rigid Body Molecular Dynamics Step
1. “Kick”: update the momenta and angular momentum vectors with known forces and torques for a half step:
\[p^k:=p^k+\tfrac h2 F^k,\quad\pi^k:=\pi^k+\tfrac h2\tau^k.\]
2. “Drift”: step forward a whole step in positions
\[q^k:=q^k+hp^k.\]
3. “Spin”: update the rotational state of the kth rigid body by the sequence of steps
\[\Theta:=\Theta^x(\tfrac h2\pi_1^k/I_1);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^y(\tfrac h2\pi_2^k/I_2);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^z(h\pi_3^k/I_3);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^y(\tfrac h2\pi_2^k/I_2);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T\]
\[\Theta:=\Theta^x(\tfrac h2\pi_1^k/I_1);\ \pi^k:=\Theta\pi^k;\ \Theta^k:=\Theta^k\Theta^T\]
4. “Kick”: update the momenta and angular momentum vectors (as in Step 1) with a half step using new forces $F^k$ and torques $\tau^k$ evaluated at the current $q,\Theta$.
corrected_json.proof_note: 原书未给独立完整证明。
context_notation: PDF195（印刷173）规定：每个刚体的 q^k 是质心位置，p^k 是线动量，π^k 是体坐标角动量，Θ^k 是3×3旋转矩阵；对每个刚体执行该步骤。π_i^k 表示第i分量，I_1,I_2,I_3 是当前刚体的主惯性矩；Lean中各体惯性可分别取 I k。
力与力矩使用上标k：\(F^k=-\partial U/\partial q^k\)，\(\tau^k=-\operatorname{rot}((\Theta^k)^T\,\partial U/\partial\Theta^k)\)。U可依赖所有刚体的位置和方向。首次kick使用当前输入构型的力/力矩，末kick在更新后的全部q,Θ处重新求值，不冻结旧力/力矩。
PDF196（印刷174）定义 \(\operatorname{rot}(A)=\operatorname{skew}^{-1}(A-A^T)\)。其分量为 \((A_{32}-A_{23},A_{13}-A_{31},A_{21}-A_{12})\)。这里原书分量从1起编号，Lean Fin 3从0起编号。

corrected_json.statement_latex:
As we mentioned in motivating the microcanonical distribution, we could alternatively view microcanonical averages as integrals with respect to the singular measure on the ambient space $\mathcal D$ defined by $\rho'_Ed\omega=Z_E^{-1}\delta[H-E]d\omega$, where $\delta$ represents the Dirac delta function. The notation $d\omega$ represents the volume element in the Euclidean space defined by all coordinates and momenta. This is the more common definition of the microcanonical distribution encountered in physics treatments.

Regardless of which formulation is adopted, we may use the probability measure to compute expectations (averages) of (suitable) functions defined on the phase space. We write such an expectation as
\[\operatorname{Av}_{H=E}(g)=\int_{\Sigma_E}g(z)d\mu_E=\int_{\mathcal D}g(z)\rho'_Ed\omega.\]
Incidentally, any such function is referred to as an observable function (or, simply, an observable) of the system in this context.

As shorthand, where the underlying space and probability density are assumed, one may write such an average more simply as $\operatorname{Av}_{H=E}(g)=\langle g\rangle$.
